cases.topic: Causes and Early Events of the French Revolution
cases.title: Tax fairness or old rules?
cases.mission: Explore why the tax system caused anger.
cases.scenario: A wealthy noble pays very little tax while a poor farmer pays a huge share of his earnings. The noble says this is the ancient law and must stay.
notes: The French population grew rapidly during the eighteenth century.
Tax rates varied widely across regions and were collected inconsistently.
Tax exemptions for the nobility and church meant the lower classes bore most of the burden.
Reform attempts were blocked by regional judicial bodies known as parlements.
This unfair tax system created deep resentment among taxpayers.

idea: France faced deep financial trouble before the revolution.
The nobility and the church enjoyed many tax exemptions.
Working people paid most of the taxes despite earning less.
Attempts to change the tax rules failed due to political blocks.
reading.example: A wealthy church official paid no land tax while a starving peasant paid high fees.
key_words: one of the three main social classes in pre-revolutionary France
freedom from having to pay or do something
a regional judicial body that registered royal laws
reading.think: Is an ancient tradition fair if it hurts most of the population?

nodes.text: The state borrowed heavily to fund wars.
Half of state revenue went on servicing debt by 1788.
Ministers proposed universal land taxes to solve the crisis.
Nobles rejected new taxes because they wanted to protect privilege.

cases.topic: Causes and Early Events of the French Revolution
cases.title: Voice for the commoners
cases.mission: Understand how the Third Estate claimed power.
cases.scenario: The king says the three social classes must meet and vote separately. The commoners refuse and declare themselves the true national assembly.
notes: The Estates-General met at Versailles in May 1789.
The Third Estate represented commoners but had no fair voting power.
Commoners demanded that all three estates meet and vote by head together.
The Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly of France.
Members took the Tennis Court Oath to stay until a constitution was agreed.

idea: The Estates-General brought together clergy, nobility, and commoners.
Commoners made up most of the population but could be easily outvoted.
Activists argued that the Third Estate represented the true nation.
Breaking away from old rules created a new source of political power.
reading.example: Commoners gathered on a tennis court after finding their meeting hall locked.
key_words: a group of people gathered for making laws or decisions
the fundamental rules and principles of a nation
counting each individual person rather than each group
reading.think: Does a majority group have the right to change the rules of government?

nodes.text: Abbé Sieyès wrote a famous pamphlet defending the Third Estate.
The king closed the meeting hall to prepare for a royal session.
Popular demonstrations forced the king to command other estates to join.

cases.topic: Causes and Early Events of the French Revolution
cases.title: Symbol of royal power
cases.mission: Examine the consequences of attacking the Bastille.
cases.scenario: Rumours spread that the king will use soldiers to close the assembly. A crowd attacks a royal fortress to find weapons and gunpowder.
notes: Rumours of military action brought angry crowds into the streets of Paris.
Soldiers of the elite guards refused to disperse the protesting crowds.
The crowd attacked the Bastille to seize stored arms and ammunition.
The fortress governor surrendered after hours of fierce fighting.
The destruction of the Bastille became a powerful symbol of ending old rule.

idea: Fears of royal violence caused panic among people in Paris.
Crowds sought weapons to defend their new political assembly.
The Bastille was a royal fortress holding arms and few prisoners.
Attacking the building showed that royal power could be challenged.
reading.example: Citizens marched on the old stone fortress and took control of its weapons.
key_words: a strong building designed to be defended against attack
the troops stationed in a fortress or town
an object that represents a deeper idea or quality
reading.think: When does a public protest turn into a revolution?

nodes.text: The king dismissed his reformist minister Necker.
Lafayette was appointed commander of the new National Guard.

cases.topic: Euthanasia and the ethics of ending life
cases.title: Defining Euthanasia
cases.mission: Understand what truly makes an act euthanasia.
cases.scenario: A doctor ends a patient life to stop severe pain. Another person kills someone for money. One is called euthanasia and one is murder.
notes: Euthanasia is the intentional ending of a life to eliminate pain and suffering.
The main motive must be for the good and best interests of the person who dies.
First, ensure the person is suffering from an incurable condition, then act with the sole intent of mercy.
Killing someone for personal gain lacks the required merciful motive, so it is just murder.
The intention to relieve suffering distinguishes true euthanasia from other intentional killings.

idea: Euthanasia means a good death.
It is done to stop severe pain.
The killer must have a merciful motive.
Killing for money is just murder.
reading.example: A doctor helps a suffering patient die peacefully.
key_words: the practice of intentionally ending life to eliminate pain
unlawful killing without a merciful reason
reading.think: What separates an act of mercy from a crime?

nodes.text: Definitions require an agent, a subject, and a clear intention.
Unintentional deaths or killings for personal gain do not count as euthanasia.
The act must use the most gentle and painless means possible.

cases.topic: Euthanasia and the ethics of ending life
cases.title: Types of Consent
cases.mission: Explore voluntary and non-voluntary choices in ending life.
cases.scenario: A patient asks a doctor to end their life. Another patient is in a coma and cannot speak. Laws treat these situations differently.
notes: Voluntary euthanasia happens when a person clearly wishes to have their life ended.
Non-voluntary euthanasia occurs when a patient is in a coma and consent is unavailable.
First, check for prior wishes, then consult doctors before allowing passive forms.
Involuntary euthanasia is done against a person will and is illegal everywhere.
Clear consent changes the legal and moral status of the procedure.

idea: Voluntary euthanasia needs the patient request.
Non-voluntary happens when the patient is in a coma.
Involuntary means against the person will.
Involuntary euthanasia is always illegal.
reading.example: A comatose patient receives passive care without speaking.
reading.think: How can we know what a patient wants if they cannot speak?

nodes.text: Active euthanasia requires the approval of doctors and counsellors.
Different countries have very different laws about medical ethics.
Assisted suicide is included under broader definitions in some nations.

cases.topic: Euthanasia and the ethics of ending life
cases.title: The Roller Coaster Idea
cases.mission: Weigh extreme concepts against real bioethics.
cases.scenario: An artist designs a device to end lives with euphoria using high forces. People debate if this creative concept fits medical ethics.
notes: The Euthanasia Coaster is a hypothetical device designed to kill passengers through lack of oxygen.
Hypothetical extreme designs test the limits of how we think about life extension and death.
First, climb to high altitudes, then trigger forces that cause loss of consciousness.
Prolonged lack of oxygen to the brain leads directly to rapid unconsciousness and death.
Artistic concepts highlight real bioethical issues without being accepted medical practice.

idea: Artists sometimes design extreme conceptual devices.
The roller coaster uses high g forces.
It causes lack of oxygen to the brain.
This highlights debates on life and death.
reading.example: A museum exhibits a scale model of a lethal ride.
key_words: suggested as an idea but not proven or real
a gas that the brain needs to function
a public display of works of art or items
reading.think: Can an extreme art project help us understand serious ethical questions?

nodes.text: Extreme g forces cause greyout and eventual loss of consciousness.
Bioethics is a very active area of research in modern science.
Public controversy occurs over the moral issues of ending life.

cases.title: Shift in Tastes
cases.mission: Distinguish general price rises from shifting consumer tastes.
cases.scenario: Cucumbers become more expensive while tomatoes get cheaper because people buy more cucumbers. A shopkeeper claims inflation is rising.
notes: Inflation is an increase in the average price of goods and services.
Inflation refers to the general trend of prices, not changes in any specific price.
Compare the price of one item to the entire consumer price index, then check if all prices are rising together.
Changes in individual prices often reflect a shift in tastes rather than a change in the value of currency.
A single product becoming expensive does not mean the purchasing power of money has dropped overall.

idea: Inflation means the average price of goods goes up.
It is measured using a price index.
When inflation happens, each unit of currency buys fewer things.
Specific price changes from changing tastes are not inflation.
reading.example: If people buy more cucumbers, cucumbers become more expensive while tomatoes get cheaper, which is just a shift in tastes.
key_words: an increase in the average price of goods and services
the amount of goods and services that money can buy
a tool used to measure the general price level
reading.think: How can you tell the difference between one expensive item and general inflation?

nodes.text: The opposite of inflation is deflation, which is a decrease in the general price level.
The consumer price index tracks the cost of a basket of common goods over time.
The inflation rate is the annualized percentage change in a general price index.
A shift in consumer preferences makes certain goods more costly without changing currency value.

cases.title: Supply Chain Stresses
cases.mission: Examine how supply shortages drive up prices.
cases.scenario: Factory shortages and transport costs make goods harder to supply. A merchant raises prices by 20 percent and blames high consumer demand alone.
notes: Global supply chain disruptions contributed to the worldwide surge in inflation.
Supply shocks involve changes in available supplies, such as during energy crises or factory shortages.
Identify the supply bottleneck, check transport costs, then measure how much input prices increased.
Supply shortages prevent the supply of goods from meeting demand, resulting in price increases.
Blaming only consumer demand ignores the real impact of production bottlenecks on final prices.

idea: Supply chain problems can cause prices to rise.
When factories close, the supply of goods goes down.
Strong consumer demand combined with low supply causes price increases.
Transportation costs also act as cost inputs for finished goods.
reading.example: During the pandemic, factory hub shortages in countries like Vietnam led to higher prices for clothes and shoes.
key_words: a sudden change in the available supplies of goods
long lasting items that consumers buy less frequently
an expense incurred to create a finished product
reading.think: Why might a shortage in factories lead to higher prices in stores?

nodes.text: Supply chain stresses increased prices for commodities and transportation.
Consumers shifting spending towards goods and away from services placed stress on supply chains.
Calculate production input costs, add transport expenses, then determine the final retail price adjustment.

cases.title: Controlling the Rate
cases.mission: Evaluate central bank responses to inflation surges.
cases.scenario: Inflation rises sharply after a period of economic stimulus. A central bank rapidly increases interest rates to cool the economy.
notes: Central banks control monetary policy by setting interest rates and carrying out open market operations.
The task of keeping the rate of inflation low and stable is given to central banks.
Observe rising inflation rates, evaluate economic stability, then decide whether to raise interest rates.
Aggressively increasing interest rates helps lower high inflation rates by cooling economic demand.
Raising interest rates too much can risk causing an economic recession.

idea: Central banks manage inflation by setting interest rates.
Most economists favor a low and steady rate of inflation.
Low inflation reduces the likelihood of economic recessions.
When inflation surges, central banks often increase interest rates.
reading.example: Following the inflation surge in recent years, almost all central banks responded by aggressively increasing interest rates.
key_words: an institution that manages a country currency and monetary policy
actions taken by a central bank to influence the economy
a period of temporary economic decline
reading.think: What are the risks of raising interest rates to stop inflation?

nodes.text: Fiscal and monetary stimulus provided by governments can contribute to demand pressures.
Lowering inflation through rate hikes can sometimes lead to a slower growing economy or a recession.
A soft landing occurs when an economy approaches target inflation while continuing to grow.

cases.title: Why memory fades
cases.mission: Understand why we forget things over time.
cases.scenario: You studied a list of facts yesterday, but today you cannot remember half of them. Your friend says memory just disappears like smoke.
notes: Memory traces weaken over time if we do not use the information.
Storage decay means the physical memory in the brain slowly fades away.
Review information regularly to keep the neural connections strong and active.
Lack of practice causes the brain to prune unused pathways.
Forgetting helps the brain clear out useless details to work efficiently.

idea: Memory naturally fades as time passes.
The brain loses details it does not need.
Unused pathways become weak and disappear.
Reviewing helps keep memories strong.
reading.example: You forget a phone number you only heard once last week.
key_words: the slow loss of information over time
the physical change in the brain left by a memory
to cut away unused connections in the brain
reading.think: Why might forgetting some things actually help your brain?

nodes.text: Synaptic connections lose strength when signals stop passing through them.
Active recall is a method where you test yourself to strengthen memory traces.
Forgetting curves show that memory loss happens fast at first, then slows down.

cases.title: Mixed up memories
cases.mission: Explore how similar memories interfere with each other.
cases.scenario: You wrote a new password, but you keep typing your old password instead. You wonder why the old memory blocks the new one.
notes: Interference happens when old and new information compete in the brain.
Proactive interference is when old memories stop you from learning new ones.
Identify the conflicting information, then practice the new detail on its own.
Similar neural pathways overlap, causing confusion during recall.
Retroactive interference occurs when new learning wipes out older memories.

idea: Similar memories can get mixed up.
Old habits block new learning sometimes.
New facts can also push out old memories.
Interference makes retrieval difficult.
reading.example: You write the wrong year on your tests at the start of January.
key_words: when memories block or mix with each other
moving forward to affect new things
looking back to affect past things
reading.think: How can you stop your old passwords from mixing with your new ones?

nodes.text: Interference is strongest when the old and new tasks are very similar.
Distinct study sessions reduce the overlap between competing memories.

The information is still in the brain, but the access path is blocked.
Search for related clues, then wait for the right cue to unlock the memory.
Missing context cues prevent the brain from finding the stored memory.
A strong hint or cue can instantly bring the forgotten memory back.

idea: Sometimes memories are stored but hard to find.
A retrieval cue helps open the path to the memory.
Context clues make searching much easier.
Not being able to recall does not mean the memory is gone.

a hint that helps trigger a memory
the situation or setting where learning happened
reading.think: Why does a small hint suddenly bring back a memory you thought was lost?

cases.topic: The Monty Hall Problem and Probability
cases.title: Three Doors
cases.mission: Understand initial chances in the game.
cases.scenario: You stand before three closed doors. Behind one door is a car, and behind the other two are goats. You pick door number one. What is your chance of winning the car?
notes: There are three doors and only one car, so your first choice has a one in three chance of success.
A probability is a number between zero and zero point nine that shows how likely an event is to happen.
Count the total number of winning doors, then divide by the total number of doors.
Because there are three total doors and only one car, your initial pick gives you a one in three chance.
You can know this by checking the fixed rules of the game show setup.

idea: Probability measures how likely an event is to happen.
Every choice starts with a baseline chance.
Counting outcomes helps find the correct odds.
Unchosen options hold different total probabilities.
reading.example: If you roll a standard die, you have a one in six chance of rolling a six.
key_words: a number that shows how likely an event is
the possibility of a particular outcome
reading.think: How does the number of total options change your chance of winning?

nodes.text: The chance of the car being behind one of the two unchosen doors is two in three.
Assume you have three doors, then calculate the odds for your single pick.
The remaining unchosen doors group together to hold a higher combined probability than your single pick.

cases.topic: The Monty Hall Problem and Probability
cases.title: The Host Reveals
cases.mission: See how new information changes the game.
cases.scenario: You pick door one. The host opens door three to show a goat. He asks if you want to switch to door two. Does this new action change your odds?
notes: The host knows where the car is and always opens a door to reveal a goat.
Information gain is the extra knowledge you get when an event happens.
Observe the host action, then note which door remains closed.
The host action adds value to the unchosen and unrevealed door because he must avoid the car.
You can trust this information because the rules state the host always follows this specific protocol.

idea: Hosts with hidden knowledge can reveal helpful clues.
Eliminating a wrong option concentrates the remaining probability.
New facts alter the value of unchosen options.
Protocol dictates how hosts must behave.
reading.example: If a teacher tells you the answer is not letter A, your chances improve on the remaining choices.
key_words: a set of rules for how an action is done
to gather together in one place
reading.think: Why does the host opening a door give you an advantage?

nodes.text: The host must always open a door that reveals a goat.
Identify the host rules, then apply them to the open door.
The host action shifts the two in three chance directly to the remaining unchosen door.

cases.topic: The Monty Hall Problem and Probability
cases.title: To Switch or Stay
cases.mission: Weigh the final strategy for the best outcome.
cases.scenario: Your friend says switching doors does not matter because two doors are left and it is a fifty fifty choice. Should you switch?
notes: Switching your choice gives you a two in three probability of winning the car.
Counterintuitive means something that goes against your first gut feeling or basic intuition.
Keep your first choice or choose to switch, then compare your win rates.
Switching wins because it captures the two in three chance of the car starting behind the unchosen doors.
You can verify this strategy using computer simulations and mathematical proofs.

idea: Counterintuitive solutions often require careful mathematical proof.
Switching uses the new information provided by the host.
Staying relies only on your very first random guess.
Testing puzzles with simulations helps convince skeptics.
reading.example: Math proofs show that changing your mind doubles your chances in this game.
key_words: contrary to what common sense would suggest
a computer model that runs tests to show results
a planned series of actions for success
reading.think: Why do so many people refuse to believe the correct strategy?

nodes.text: Staying with your initial choice wins in only one out of three possibilities.
Test both staying and switching, then record the final win rates.
Switching is a different action from choosing at random because it uses previous information.

cases.title: History and Growth
cases.mission: Understand how palm oil became a major industry.
cases.scenario: Your friend says palm oil has always been Malaysia's main crop. You check the facts and find it was introduced by the British in the 1870s as an ornamental plant before commercial farming started in 1917.
notes: Palm oil trees were brought to British Malaya by the British government in the early 1870s.
The first commercial palm oil cultivation started in Selangor in 1917 at Tennamaran Estate.
Palm oil cultivation increased significantly in the 1960s to reduce dependency on rubber and tin.
The government introduced land settlement schemes to eradicate poverty among local people.
Malaysia became the world largest exporter of palm oil in the same period.

idea: Palm oil trees came to Malaysia long ago.
Farming started slowly on estates.
The government later expanded the industry to help the economy.
This growth changed land use across the country.
reading.example: The government planted more palm oil trees in the 1960s to reduce reliance on rubber and tin.
key_words: growing crops on a large scale
adding new products to reduce economic risk
a large area of land with one owner
reading.think: Why do governments encourage farmers to grow new crops?

nodes.text: Diversification programs lowered economic risk by creating multiple export products.
Land settlement schemes gave plots to smallholders to farm palm oil.
Increased farming led to higher export volumes globally.

cases.title: Environmental Rules
cases.mission: Examine the environmental impact of palm oil expansion.
cases.scenario: A policy maker claims that expanding palm oil farms has no environmental cost. You learn that deforestation concerns led the government to pledge keeping half the land as forest cover.
notes: Palm oil production is vital for the economy of Malaysia.
The European Commission concluded that palm oil cultivation causes excessive deforestation.
The Malaysian government pledged in 2010 to retain at least half of the nation as forest cover.
Deforestation concerns led to international trade disputes and proposed bans.
Sustainable practices are required to balance economic needs with environmental protection.

idea: Palm oil is very important for the national economy.
Farming can cause serious deforestation and habitat loss.
Governments try to balance farming with forest preservation.
Other countries may restrict imports due to environmental worries.
reading.example: The Malaysian government promised to keep half the land as forest cover to address environmental concerns.
key_words: clearing a wide area of trees
a fuel made from plant oils
reading.think: How can countries balance economic growth with protecting nature?

nodes.text: Forest cover retention limits the total land available for new plantations.
Environmental rules create friction between producer countries and importing nations.
Certification schemes help verify if palm oil is produced sustainably.

cases.title: Labor and Trade
cases.mission: Analyze how labor issues affect international trade.
cases.scenario: An investor says that labor practices do not affect product sales. You find that the United States banned imports from certain companies after investigations into forced labor.
notes: The United States banned palm oil imports from Sime Darby after investigations into forced labor.
Malaysia accounted for 31 percent of United States palm oil imports in the 2020 fiscal year.
India restricted refined palm oil imports following political disagreements.
Companies must address labor violations to lift import bans.
Ethical standards directly influence global market access for agricultural products.

idea: Labor practices are critical for international trade.
Foreign governments can ban goods made with forced labor.
Political tensions can also disrupt major export markets.
Companies must fix labor issues to restore trade.
reading.example: The United States issued a ban on palm oil imports from companies linked to forced labor.
key_words: a penalty for breaking international rules
bringing goods into a country from abroad
reading.think: What responsibilities do importing countries have regarding labor conditions abroad?

nodes.text: Labor investigations reveal hidden human rights violations in supply chains.
Import bans reduce export revenue for producer nations.
Implementing remedial actions allows companies to apply for ban lifts.
